row.overview: Little Annapurna (8,485 ft) is a granite summit in the Core (Upper) Enchantments, Stuart Range, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, immediately south of the Enchantment Lakes basin near Isolation and Tranquil Lakes. It was named by Ellensburg's Sherpa Climbing Club for its resemblance to the Himalayan Annapurna massif. The North Slopes route is the easiest way up the peak, an enjoyable Class 2-3 scramble typically approached via Aasgard Pass, finishing with a short 3rd-class step onto the small summit pedestal and views of Dragontail Peak, the Knitting/Nightmare Needles, and the Enchantment Lakes.
row.beta: From the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trailhead, hike to Colchuck Lake and grind up the steep boulder-and-scree gully of Aasgard Pass to reach the upper Enchantment basin. From the pass, head roughly south-southwest past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes toward Little Annapurna's northeast ridge, then follow cairns up open granite slabs and talus on the peak's north side to the summit -- one of three rocky high points on the ridge, with the true summit being the middle one. The line itself involves minimal exposure and only occasional Class 3 moves, but Aasgard Pass is the physical and route-finding crux of the day.
row.turnaround: The route is short, so weather is the deciding factor. Be off the open summit plateau before afternoon storms, which can build quickly over the Enchantments.
row.face: Standard route: upper Enchantments basin and the peak's north/west-facing slopes, ascending near (west of) the northeast ridge
row.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
row.comms: Parties report no cell service at the trailhead or anywhere along the approach and route; a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) is recommended for emergencies.
row.descent: Reverse the NE-flank scramble to the plateau, then retrace the route back over Aasgard Pass and down to Colchuck Lake and the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail. Early season the Aasgard Pass headwall can often be glissaded; by late summer it is loose talus/scree, and the descent is typically slower and harder on the knees than the climb up.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive Eightmile Road (FR-7601) to its end at the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake trailhead, about 3,500 ft. Overnight stays in the Colchuck Zone need a quota wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stuart Lake Trail #1599 about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599.1 splits left and south. Continue roughly 1.8 miles more, crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet, to the lake at 5,570 ft. This is the last easy, reliable water, so fill here because there is none above.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.directions: Skirt the lake's south and east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the foot of the obvious steep gully and headwall at the head of the lake. Aasgard gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping; cairns get knocked over and the path splits into several use trails, so keep re-picking the line toward the notch. Firm snow and ice can linger into July, making an axe and sometimes crampons worthwhile on what is otherwise a scramble.

waypoints.name: Core Enchantments
waypoints.directions: From the pass, cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

waypoints.name: Base of north slopes
waypoints.directions: Near the far end of the meadows, watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right, to the west, toward Little Annapurna. If you cross a stream and pass a toilet sign you have gone by the junction and should backtrack.

waypoints.name: Little Annapurna summit
waypoints.directions: Above here it is a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths rather than a trail. Take the line of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east side, switchbacking and scrambling at low 3rd class at most. The true summit is the middle of three rocky high points along the crest.

row.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed. An ice axe is worthwhile early in the season for snow on the upper slopes, and trekking poles help on the talus.
pro_tips: Combine it with nearby Core summits in one outing.
Carry an axe early season for the upper snow.

row.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing; movement is unroped scrambling. The challenge is minimal beyond basic route-finding and staying back from the south edge.
row.best_season: Late June/July through early October for a snow-free scramble; the Aasgard Pass headwall and upper slopes often hold snow well into July, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is recommended early season. Late September brings the Enchantment basin's famous larch color along with its heaviest crowds and permit competition.
row.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping, cairns are frequently knocked down and the path braids into several use-trails, and well into summer it can still hold firm snow/ice that makes an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) worthwhile even though the route is otherwise a scramble. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,800-7,841 ft, ~5.3 mi from the trailhead). Beyond the pass, cross the grey talus/glacial-till 'moonscape' of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets. Near the far end of these meadows watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna — crossing a stream and passing a toilet sign means you've overshot the junction. From there the route is more a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths than a trail; pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling (low 3rd class at most) to the 8,485-ft summit. Trailhead-to-summit totals run about 15-16 miles and 5,000-5,800 ft. Hazards: no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet, so fill up there; loose rock and rockfall potential on Aasgard Pass and the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun/thunderstorm exposure on the open talus above the pass; and early/mid-season snow on the pass creating slip-and-slide fall hazard.
row.descent_text: Reverse the North Slopes: downclimb the low-3rd-class/class-2 slabs and talus on the peak's east side back to the col/basin, pick up the braided boot paths back through the Brisingamen Lakelets meadows, and rejoin the Core Zone trail past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes to Aasgard Pass. This is a scramble walk-off in both directions — no rope, rack, or rappelling is used on the standard North Slopes line; parties simply describe reversing the ascent, and the peak is often characterized as little more than a steep class 2 hike. The one genuine descent-specific hazard is Aasgard Pass itself: down-climbing its ~2,000 ft of loose scree and talus in the afternoon (often with the sun having softened any remaining snow, and other parties ascending below) is a common cause of rockfall incidents and slips — down-climb deliberately, stay out of others' fall line, and only glissade if a real, clean snow chute with a safe runout is in (by mid-to-late summer the pass is usually bare, exposed talus rather than snow). From the base of the pass, retrace the trail around Colchuck Lake and down the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead. Rappels: 0.
row.bail: Retreat is trivial by reversing the scramble at any point, with no committing terrain. The only real caution is keeping well back from the abrupt south edge of the summit plateau.

access.fees: $6 non-refundable lottery application fee; overnight camping fee of $5 per person per night (May 15-October 31); a Northwest Forest Pass is required for trailhead parking at the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead.
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. access.rules: Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft and within 0.5 mile of any lake, which effectively bans fires along the entire approach and on the peak; dogs are prohibited throughout the Enchantment Permit Area; group size is capped at 8 in the Colchuck/Stuart zones; camp only at established sites on rock, gravel, or sand.
access.permit: Overnight camping anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area (including the Colchuck and Stuart zones used to approach Little Annapurna, and the Core Zone around Isolation/Tranquil Lakes) requires a permit via Recreation.gov, allocated mostly through the advance lottery held mid-February to March 1 (results posted mid-March), with a limited number of rolling 7-day-window/walk-up releases through the rest of the season.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's LEFT of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.

Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself

No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the FAR END of the meadows, watch for an UNSIGNED path forking RIGHT (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream AND pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the SOUTHEAST and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad north-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's LEFT (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head SOUTH toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad north-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the LEFT (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a north-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.

climbing_route.label: North slabs and talus to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths rather than a trail: pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling to the 8,485-ft summit. Loose rock and rockfall potential on the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun and thunderstorm exposure on the open talus; no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

name: The Direct North Ridge w/ Gendarme
findings: r038.json: The route documents two genuine approaches (Esmeralda/Goat Pass, marked primary, and Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek), and waypoint[0]'s own directions explicitly label that pin as the Icicle-side start and tell the party the Teanaway side is a different drive; two labelled options, not a wrong fact.

row.name: The Direct North Ridge w/ Gendarme
row.fa: North Ridge (original line, bypassing the Great Gendarme): Don Claunch & John Rupley, September 9, 1956. Complete North Ridge, via the lower ridge's west side: Fred Beckey & Steve Marts, 1963. First ascent climbing directly over the Great Gendarme: James Wickwire & Fred Stanley, 1964. Direct lower-ridge start variation (from the true toe): Mead Hargis & Jay Ossiander, 1970
hazards: The gendarme-bypass gully (rappelling right/west at its base) is prone to rockfall on dirty rock and is not recommended; the upper mountain is almost always shaded and can be icy/cold on the crux pitches
Documented accident, July 2020: a climber was struck by rockfall near the top of the route, took a long fall, and required roughly 24 hours to rescue after failed helicopter extraction attempts.
row.overview: The full-length version of the North Ridge, starting at the true toe rather than the notch, adding roughly 800 vertical feet and a sustained 5.9+ opening lieback before joining the standard North Ridge line up through the Great Gendarme.
row.beta: Three opening pitches off a ledge ~150 ft above the toe — including an awkward 5.8 squeeze slot and a striking, sustained 5.9+ lieback crack — join the standard North Ridge; from there roughly 11 more pitches of exposed 4th-to-mid-5th ridge climbing on excellent granite lead to the Great Gendarme (two 5.9 pitches: a fingers/hands dihedral and an offwidth), then blocky 4th/low-5th terrain to the summit.
row.turnaround: A full-value Grade IV outing — recorded ascents range from about 9 hours of pure climbing to 15-40 hours car-to-car including bivies. Set a firm turnaround before the Gendarme and carry bivy gear as a contingency.
row.rappels: ~75 ft rappel around the Great Gendarme if bypassing; otherwise walk off via Cascadian Couloir or Sherpa Glacier/Sherpa Pass
row.face: North Ridge (complete, base to summit via the 1970 direct start)
row.permit: Depends on the approach. Over Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead you are outside the Enchantment Permit Area: the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit covers day and overnight use, with no lottery. Via Mountaineer Creek from the Stuart Lake trailhead, camps are in the Enchantment Permit Area's Stuart Zone, where overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need only the free self-issued permit.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the ridge.
row.descent: Cascadian Couloir (most common) or Sherpa Glacier/Sherpa Pass (faster, early season, north side)

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (Eightmile Creek Rd #7601)
waypoints.note: Trail #1599 up Icicle/Eightmile Creek, then cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the base of the ridge.
waypoints.directions: This pin is the Icicle-side start, not the Teanaway one. Drive Eightmile Creek Road (FS 7601) to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, about 3,400 ft, where Trail #1599 up Icicle/Eightmile Creek leaves the lot; the approach then goes cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the toe of the ridge. If you are coming at the ridge the other way, over Ingalls Pass and Goat Pass, that is a different drive to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, so make sure you and your partner agree on the trailhead before you leave town.

waypoints.name: Base of North Ridge (glacier moat)
waypoints.note: Gain the ridge crest via the moat beside the Sherpa/Ice Cliff Glaciers; complete ridge route starts here.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart summit
waypoints.note: Crux is the Great Gendarme (5.9 offwidth) about 500 ft below the summit; a short rappel bypasses it around the base.

timing.recommendedStart: Very early alpine start (a recorded ascent left the trailhead at 5:24am)

row.detailed_rack: Cams 0.3-3in (doubles 0.4-2in, optional #4 for the Gendarme offwidth), one set of nuts (offsets recommended), 8-12 alpine draws; optional ice axe/crampons/helmet for approach snow.
what_to_bring: Extra food/water for a long day
pro_tips: The lower 3 pitches are a real technical crux (5.9+ sustained lieback) — don't underestimate them
Decide on the Gendarme bypass vs. direct finish before you're below it
row.watch_out:
Loose rock and sometimes crumbly black lichen on rock at times
Alternative bypass gully NOT recommended - involves climbing dirty rock prone to rockfall
Gendarme section almost always in shade - can be very cold or even icy, creating hypothermia risk and icy climbing conditions
Significant complex terrain: 'parties have accidentally taken wrong descent path' - disorientation hazard
Seasonal constraints: snow patches affect water availability at notch (8,200 ft)
Multiple approach/descent options involve glacier travel (Sherpa, Stuart glaciers) that become 'too difficult to navigate' as season progresses
Route quality varies - some sections clean, others lichen-covered and unstable
20 pitches of mostly 5th class climbing with mixed terrain
Helmet essential due to rockfall concern
Complex terrain and poor visibility increase navigation challenges especially during descent
row.pro_needs: A standard alpine rack sized up for the offwidth crux; natural pro (horns, slung blocks) supplements the rack on the long ridge sections.
row.best_season: July through September; a lingering ice/snow patch in the gully below the Great Gendarme can persist into midsummer.
row.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls. For the Cascadian Couloir and South Headwall, turn right onto the Longs Pass Trail at the junction about 1.7 miles in, climb to Longs Pass (about 6,250 ft) near mile 2.9, and descend the rocky climbers' trail on the far side to Ingalls Creek, cross on a log bridge, and follow the climbers' path up the meadow into the base of the Cascadian Couloir (South Headwall lies further up-basin via the same drainage). For West Ridge, the North Ridge routes, and the South Face (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), instead stay on the Ingalls Way Trail over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3) and continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft) — the South Face wall with the Gorillas routes sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, while West Ridge and North Ridge climbers continue over or along Goat Pass toward their respective start points. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek depending on the objective. The North Ridge routes can also be reached from the opposite (Mountaineer Creek) side.
row.descent_text: The Cascadian Couloir is the most common descent — a long traverse south then a loose, sustained scree/talus descent to Ingalls Creek. On the north side, the Sherpa Glacier is quicker and more direct in early season for parties based at a Mountaineer Creek camp; alternatively descend 3rd-class terrain around the south side of Sherpa Peak to Sherpa Pass and glissade a snow slope. A West Ridge downclimb is reported as tedious and not recommended.
row.bail: Retreat is difficult once established above the first few pitches; the short rappel around the Great Gendarme is the main planned bail/bypass option below the final headwall.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from a big ledge about 150 ft above the true toe of the ridge. Climb easy ground and a lieback to a small pine, then continue into an awkward squeeze slot, 5.8 and considerably harder with a pack on. Pitch breaks vary between parties here; belay on the ledge above the slot.
Face climbing on good granite to a comfortable ledge at the foot of the long crack on the left. Moderate and well protected; it sets up the belay for the crux pitch.

The technical crux of the whole route: a striking, sustained lieback crack on the left that goes on for a long way, ending with a pull over a small roof to a belay ledge. Pumpy and insecure with alpine packs. Parties who cannot free it often aid through the crux.

A short pitch that finishes the steep lower buttress. Above it, the ridge eases and the simul-climbing begins. Take note of the terrain above before pulling the rope, since route-finding from here to the notch is by the cleanest path.

Long simul-climbing blocks of 3rd class to 5.6 up and right along the ridge to the large notch at about 8,200 ft, where the Stuart Glacier approach joins. Rock off the most-travelled line is loose and lichen-covered, so follow the cleanest path. The notch has bivy sites and, earlier in the season, water from snowmelt.

From the notch stay on the left (east) side, then follow an easy ramp to the crest. The ridge narrows to an exposed knife-edge, taken on its west side, with short 5.5 laybacks and one 5.7 move. A superb 5.5 slab split by a crack comes just before the Gendarme. Most parties simul-climb most of this upper ridge.

A steep fingers-and-hands dihedral with laybacks and underclings, with good rests between the harder sections, to the top of a pillar. Given grades range from 5.8 to 5.9. The Gendarme is almost always shaded and can be cold, wet or iced after bad weather. Bypass option: a bolted rappel down the west side, then a dirty, rockfall-prone gully; not recommended.

Traverse to the offwidth and climb it. It is steep and intimidating from below but has solid holds and fist jams inside; given grades range from 5.8+ to 5.9+. A 3.5–4 in cam is essential, and a second one makes it much safer. Belay above once the angle eases.

Above the Gendarme, trend right on an airy traverse back to the crest at a small saddle. Climb a short 5.7 hand crack (some parties find a 5.8 move), then lower-angle broken ground leads to the summit (9,415 ft). The descent is the Cascadian Couloir to the south, or the Sherpa Glacier for a north-side camp.

row.itinerary: Typically done as a long single day by fast parties (simul-climbing) or over 2-3 days with a bivy on the ridge for parties pitching it out fully.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Stuart zone), required May 15 to October 31 — limited, not free
overnight_permit.where: Apply to the advance lottery on Recreation.gov in late February; leftover and daily permits are released on Recreation.gov after the lottery. No permit needed for a day climb or outside the season.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek. Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp. From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock. The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at an entry on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul; best early, while the Sherpa Glacier still gives a straightforward descent back to this side
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
KEEP THE ICE CLIFF GLACIER ON YOUR LEFT AND WALK UNTIL THE ROCK STOPS YOU. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a BIG LEDGE about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the SOUTH side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse EAST below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY ABOVE THE MORAINE MOUND AND KEEP TRAVERSING. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking DOWN onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

ARRIVAL: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

bivy.name: Mountaineer Creek basin below the Sherpa Glacier
bivy.notes: The standard base for the north side of Mount Stuart. Leave the Stuart Lake trail before the final switchbacks, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the south fork of Mountaineer Creek to the flat valley below the Sherpa and Stuart glaciers.
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Stuart zone) from May 15 to October 31
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites on flat ground in the basin

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

row.name: South Slopes
hazards: Lingering snowfields on the upper bowl/ridge into July — can obscure the route and create fall/glissade hazard on steep sections
Afternoon thunderstorms with lightning exposure on the open ridge and summit
Loose talus and blocky terrain above ~6,000 ft — rockfall risk onto parties below

Long, mostly waterless upper approach — carry sufficient water
row.overview: Navaho Peak is the fourth-highest summit in the Teanaway high country and sits on the boundary of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, on the Kittitas/Chelan county line about 2 miles northeast of Earl Peak and 1.3 miles west of Three Brothers. The South Slopes/Southwest Ridge line is the standard non-technical route: a long approach up Stafford Creek to an open bowl and ridge system, then a broad talus-and-heather scramble to a small summit (room for only 4-5 people) with wide views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, Sherpa Peak, Earl Peak, and Mount Rainier.
row.beta: The standard route follows the Stafford Creek Trail to Navaho Pass, then picks up the old County Line Trail heading east to intersect Navaho's south ridge; from there it's roughly a 700-foot Class 2 ridge scramble on a boot path to the summit. Reported round-trip stats vary by source from about 11-14 miles with 4,000-4,300 feet of gain depending on the exact line taken. A known shortcut leaves the main trail about 3 miles in, where two creek forks meet, and climbs directly to the saddle below the peak's southeast ridge, cutting roughly 2 miles off the round trip.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time (e.g., early-to-mid afternoon) given the long, mostly open ridge above treeline with no quick escape from lightning — East Cascades thunderstorms typically build in the afternoon.
row.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent for most of the approach and at the summit given the remote, forested/alpine terrain of the Teanaway backcountry; do not rely on a cell signal for emergencies.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 9703; ~20-car lot with pit toilet, Northwest Forest Pass or $5 self-issue fee required; trail has seen closures for Labor Mountain Fire damage so check current USFS alerts before going.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Teanaway River Road to 29 Pines Campground, bear right where the pavement ends, then turn onto Stafford Creek Road and follow it a couple of miles to where it ends at the trailhead. The last stretch is dirt and washboarded but passable to low-clearance cars in dry conditions.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek crossing, Stafford Creek Meadows
waypoints.note: Stream crossing in the meadows on Trail #1359; last reliable water before the drier climb toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1359 leaves the lot at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek most of the way. A short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The forest stays open and the grade never gets hard before the trail reaches the marshy meadow ground.

waypoints.name: Standup Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1359 meets the Standup Creek Trail about 2 miles below Navaho Pass; continue straight/left on #1359 toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Stay on Stafford Creek Trail #1359, still gaining gradually along the creek, to the signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369).

waypoints.name: Upper meadow camp
waypoints.note: Established camp area in the upper meadow (elev/dist interpolated between the 4,800 ft creek crossing and the pass); common overnight staging spot before the steep push above.
waypoints.directions: Continue on Trail #1359 above the junction; the trail opens out into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream — another water source, and the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days.

waypoints.name: Navaho Pass
waypoints.note: Junction with the old County Line Trail (Cascade Creek Trail #1217); barren, rocky 'moon-scape' terrain with big Enchantments views, but very exposed to wind for camping.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow the trail leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky slope for the last stretch, gaining roughly 500 ft to the saddle. There is no water and essentially no shade on this section, and on the dry east side it bakes on a warm afternoon.

waypoints.name: South ridge scramble path
waypoints.note: Steep climber's path of loose scree and dirt gaining the south ridge; snow patches can linger into July, making poles/microspikes worthwhile.
waypoints.directions: From the pass turn east and follow the crest trail a short way toward the peak, then leave it where a boot path breaks off uphill onto the south ridge. The path is loose scree over dirt and steepens quickly, so poles earn their keep and it is easy to push rock down onto anyone below you.

waypoints.name: Navaho Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,223 ft on the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary; panoramic views of the Enchantments and Stuart Range.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest up for a bit over 600 ft of gain on broken rock and scree; the scrambling stays easy Class 2 with hands wanted only occasionally. Stay on the ridge line rather than dropping onto the looser slopes on either side, which are steeper than they look from above.

Great fall outing with golden larches en route
row.best_season: Late June openings are possible in low-snow years, but snow often lingers into July and can turn the final scramble into route-finding on snow — August and September typically offer the driest, most straightforward conditions. October brings golden larches on the lower approach and clear, cool weather but shorter days. Regardless of season, check current Forest Service closure status before going (see access.closures).
row.approach: Start at the Stafford Creek Trailhead (Trail #1359), Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, at the end of Stafford Creek Road (FR 9703), which leaves North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) past 29 Pines Campground — a small, often-overflowing lot for roughly 20 cars (Northwest Forest Pass required). From the trailhead, Stafford Creek Trail #1359 climbs at a gentle-to-moderate grade through dry ponderosa/lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek for the first mile (a short rerouted, steeper switchback section around 0.5 mile bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread). The trail continues gaining gradually along the creek — figure roughly 3,000 ft of gain spread over the approach — reaching a signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) at about 3.5–3.8 miles; this crossing of Stafford Creek is the last reliable, easy water source before the high country and is worth topping off here. Bear right (east/north) at the junction to stay on the Navaho Pass approach. Around 4.5 miles the trail opens into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with established campsites and a feeder stream — the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days, and another water source. Beyond camp the trail crosses the barren, eroded 'Moon Landing' stretch (sparse vegetation, serpentine/greenstone talus) before a final push to Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft) around mile 5.5. A commonly used shortcut leaves the main trail where two creek forks merge around the 3-mile mark, climbing steep, loose slopes directly up the northeast-facing drainage to the col below Navaho's southeast ridge — it saves close to 2 miles of trail hiking but is steeper, unmaintained, and involves loose scree/dirt, so most parties use it only for one direction of the trip. Total car-to-summit is on the order of 11–13 miles round trip with about 4,000–4,200 ft of gain depending on which junction/shortcut combination is used. Note: this trail corridor has had closures tied to the Labor Mountain Fire and storm damage; Forest Service order 06-17-03-2026-14 closed Stafford Creek Trail #1359 from May 20 through December 31, 2026 unless rescinded sooner, but that order is no longer posted on the Okanogan-Wenatchee alerts page (checked September 26, 2026) — verify current trail status with the Cle Elum Ranger District (509-852-1100) before heading in. A second off-trail variant leaves the trail right after the Stafford Creek crossing and climbs directly into the open bowl between Earl Peak and Navaho Peak to about 5,000 ft, scrambles north to the ridgeline near 6,000 ft, then follows the west/southwest ridge to the summit — a different line than the northeast-drainage shortcut.
row.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: drop off the summit back down the broad south/southeast ridge to Navaho Pass (easy Class 2 scrambling, no rope or rappelling needed), then rejoin Stafford Creek Trail #1359 and retrace it past the Moon Landing section, the meadow camp/water source, the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) junction at ~3.5–3.8 miles, and back down along Stafford Creek to the trailhead. Parties who used the creek-fork shortcut on the way up sometimes descend the standard pass-and-trail route instead (or vice versa) to make a rough loop, but both options are plain hiking/scrambling terrain — there is no rappelling on this route. Watch for loose scree and dirt on the steeper shortcut drainage if descending that way, and expect possible lingering snow near the pass and on the upper ridge into early-mid summer, which can make the descent line slicker than the ascent.
row.bail: Reversible anywhere on the nontechnical route.

approach_variants.name: Stafford Creek Trail #1359 to Navaho Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the small road-end lot, Trail #1359 leaves at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek; a short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The creek crossing in the meadows is the last easy water and worth topping off at. Stay on #1359 at the signed Standup Creek Trail junction, and the trail opens into a large marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream and established campsites — the usual overnight base. Above the meadow the tread leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky, sparsely vegetated slope for the last stretch to the pass.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow patches linger on the upper ridge into July, when poles and light traction are worthwhile.
hazards: No water and essentially no shade above the meadows, on ground that bakes on a warm afternoon
Loose scree over dirt on the climbers' path onto the ridge, steepening quickly and easy to push down onto a party below
Lingering snow patches into July
Slopes on either flank of the summit ridge are looser and steeper than they look from above
The trail corridor has been closed for fire and storm damage — check current status before driving in
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SUMMIT PATH IS NOW MORE WORN THAN THE TRAIL IT LEAVES, AND THE WRONG TURN HAS A NAME. Navaho Pass is unmistakable ground — small, rocky, sparsely vegetated and wind-exposed, with the Stuart Range filling the view — and it is where the trail meets the old crest trail along the county line. Head EAST out of the pass, paralleling the range. The old boot-path junction that descriptions still mention has effectively vanished: the beaten track now IS the summit path, more worn than the crest trail beside it, so the thing to look for is the most-used tread rather than a faint branch. If instead you follow the connecting ridge LEFT from the pass, you are heading for Wrong Turn Peak, which is what it is called and why. Two more confusions worth knowing: the prominent peak straight ahead on the walk in is Little Navaho, not this one, and the final ridge throws up several false tops before the true summit, which is small — barely higher than a rocky outcrop just east of it. On the way down, do not follow the southeast ridge all the way toward Little Navaho; there are cliffs below it.

climbing_route.label: South ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From Navaho Pass (~6,000 ft), leave the maintained trail and traverse/climb east along the broad south ridge of Navaho Peak: an easy, mostly open scramble on rock and heather with no technical exposure, gaining the final 1,100–1,200 ft to the 7,223 ft summit over about 0.8–1 mile.

bivy.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
bivy.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
bivy.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

row.overview: Red Mountain (5,890 ft) is the distinctive rust-red peak rising above Commonwealth Basin, 3 miles north of Snoqualmie Pass in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. One of the popular 'Snoqualmie Ten,' it's a non-technical but genuinely loose scramble: the red color comes from iron-oxide staining on heavily fractured volcanic rock, which is notoriously crumbly and rockfall-prone despite the peak's benign reputation as a walk-up.
row.beta: Approach via Pacific Crest Trail north from Exit 52, following Commonwealth Creek trail to the base of the mountain. The final 1,000-1,100 feet ascends the west-facing slope at 30-40 degrees inclination. Most loose rock has been removed by frequent traffic. South-facing sections feature more solid red volcanic slabs. Winter ascents are possible with snow coverage on the southwest ridge when avalanche conditions are stable.
row.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround in early-to-mid afternoon: the upper slope is more dangerous to descend in fading light, and July–August afternoons can bring thunderstorms over the Cascade crest with no shelter on the open summit rock.
row.comms: T-Mobile provides the best cellular coverage in the Snoqualmie Pass area at 92%+ availability. Other carriers (AT&T, Verizon) also available but with variable coverage. Terrain and weather can degrade signal. Sat communication devices recommended for emergencies on longer trips into the wilderness.

row.pro_needs: None — no rack, rope, or protection needed; this is unroped Class 2-3 scrambling on both standard lines.
row.best_season: July through October is the reliable window; snow typically lingers in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper slope into early-to-mid July, and the fractured rock becomes genuinely unsafe when wet, so a dry-rock, snow-free window from late July through September is the sweet spot. October is climbable but daylight and weather windows shrink fast and early snow can arrive by month's end.
row.approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 — this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Follow the PCT for roughly 2–2.5 miles of well-graded, well-maintained trail through old-growth forest with blueberry and salmonberry understory, gaining a gentle ~2,000 ft over the first 4.5 miles combined. At the signed junction, leave the PCT and turn left (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, following it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek in the basin, which is the one reliable natural water source on the approach (treat before drinking) — carry enough water above this point since the final scramble slopes are dry. As the trail levels out near a small tarn/pond below Red Mountain's west slope, watch for a cairn planted in the middle of the path — this marks the scramble takeoff point where you leave the maintained trail. An alternate, rougher approach follows the older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin Trail starting about 20 yards up from the parking lot, switchbacking directly up into the basin and rejoining near the same trail split (bear right toward Red Pass); it's shorter but harder to follow and not recommended in poor visibility. From the cairn, pick up a boot path climbing the west slope; the track is intermittent and easy to lose on scree, so stay close to the ridge crest on climber's right (south) if you're unsure of the line. The final roughly 900 ft over the last half mile is the crux of the approach: a 30–40° slope of fractured red (iron-stained) rock, loose scree, heather, and scattered alpine trees, alternating Class 2 and low Class 3 scrambling with no real exposure — hands are needed intermittently but it's non-technical. This upper slope holds snow into early summer and can present avalanche/glissade hazard in spring conditions; by mid-to-late summer it's typically dry but still loose and slick when wet.
row.descent_text: No rope or rappelling is used on the standard route — this is a pure walk/scramble descent. Most parties reverse the ascent line down the west-slope boot path back to the cairn and Commonwealth Creek Trail, then retrace the Commonwealth Creek Trail and PCT back to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend via the southwest ridge crest before dropping back into the boot-path drainage, which can offer more solid footing than the loose central scree the boot path sometimes follows — either line rejoins the same trail system before the pond. The overriding descent hazard is loose, fractured rock underfoot (a helmet is strongly recommended for the whole party, not just the leader, since Red Mountain's red rock is notoriously fractured and easy to kick loose onto climbers below); keep the group tight and avoid spreading out on the open scree. Do not attempt to traverse east/south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Catwalk as a shortcut — that terrain quickly becomes Class 3/4 and cliffs out without a rope. Once back on the boot path, staying close to the ridge crest on the way down (rather than cutting straight down the gut of the scree slope) both preserves the trail and reduces rockfall risk to other parties.
row.bail: Retreat is simple at any point — reverse the boot path back down to the basin pond and rejoin the maintained PCT/Commonwealth Creek Trail. No technical descent or fixed retreat gear needed.

crowds.estimatePerSeason: High for an alpine scramble — Red Mountain sits right off I-90 at Snoqualmie Pass via the popular Commonwealth Basin/PCT trailhead. Climbers describe 6+ other parties on the scramble portion on a single weekend day, and locals explicitly recommend a weekday ascent to avoid the crush.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 - this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north.

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail to the cairn by the tarn, then the west-slope boot path
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass West, I-90 exit 52. Follow the rerouted PCT north roughly 2 to 2.5 miles of well-graded trail through old growth. At the signed junction, turn LEFT (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, and follow it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek, the one reliable water on the approach — fill up there, because the scramble slopes above are dry.

An older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin trail leaves about 20 yards up from the parking lot and switchbacks directly into the basin, rejoining near the same split. It is shorter, harder to follow, and not recommended in poor visibility.

About 12.9 km round trip and 2,900 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Snow lingers in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper slope into early-to-mid July, and the fractured rock is genuinely unsafe wet, so late July to September is the sweet spot
hazards: Rockfall on loose, heavily fractured red rock, with documented close calls near the summit
Slick, dangerous rock when wet — an easy class 2 slope becomes unsafe in rain
Route-finding above the basin tarn where maintained trail becomes a cairned boot path
Lingering snow and postholing into early summer
Cliffed-out class 3-4 ground if a party tries to shortcut east toward the Kendall Katwalk
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TAKEOFF IS MARKED BY A CAIRN PLANTED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PATH, AND THAT IS THE ARRIVAL TEST. As the trail levels out near a small tarn below Red Mountain's west slope, a cairn sits in the middle of the tread. That is where the scramble leaves the maintained trail. A cairn off to one side is not it; this one is in the way, deliberately.

FROM THE CAIRN, WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO: a boot path climbs the west slope. It is intermittent and easy to lose on scree. THE RULE WHEN YOU LOSE IT IS TO STAY CLOSE TO THE RIDGE CREST ON CLIMBERS' RIGHT — the south side. That single rule replaces route-finding for the whole upper slope, and it also keeps you off the loose gut of the scree where you would be kicking rock onto people.

WHAT THE LAST 900 FT SHOULD FEEL LIKE: a 30 to 40 degree slope of fractured, iron-stained RED rock, loose scree, heather and scattered alpine trees, alternating class 2 and low class 3, with no real exposure. Hands needed intermittently. If you are on genuinely exposed ground with real fall consequence, you have drifted off the line.

AND THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE, WHICH IS ABOUT THE DESCENT BUT BELONGS HERE: do NOT traverse east or south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Katwalk as a shortcut. That terrain becomes class 3 and 4 and cliffs out without a rope.

HONEST NOTE ON THE ROCK: helmets are for the whole party, not just a leader. Red Mountain's rock is notoriously fractured and there are documented close calls with softball- and grapefruit-sized rock near the summit.

climbing_route.label: Boot path up the west slope
climbing_route.notes: From the cairn planted in the middle of the path near the tarn, pick up a boot path climbing the west slope. The track is intermittent and easy to lose on scree, so stay close to the ridge crest on climber's right (south) if you're unsure of the line.

climbing_route.label: Final 900 ft of red rock and scree
climbing_route.notes: The final roughly 900 ft over the last half mile is a 30-40° slope of fractured red (iron-stained) rock, loose scree, heather, and scattered alpine trees, with no real exposure — hands are needed intermittently but it's non-technical. This upper slope holds snow into early summer and can present avalanche/glissade hazard in spring conditions; by mid-to-late summer it's typically dry but still loose and slick when wet.

bivy.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
bivy.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
bivy.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

row.name: Drilling Me Softly
hazards: Loose and sharp rock is a known issue at this recently-developed alpine sport crag.
The approach and crag sit in a remote basin with no cell coverage, so any injury means a long self-evacuation or SAR response.
row.overview: Alpine sport climb at Sofa King Buttress in The Citidel area.
row.beta: Fully bolted 5.10b/c sport pitch on Sofa King Buttress, positioned as the leftmost route on the wall. The line (FA party Wylie Moreshead) is known for the sheer variety of technique packed into one pitch rather than a single hard crux — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacking, jugs, crimps and underclings. Protected by 12 bolts to chain anchors at the top; photos of the route show the crux section and a rest stance before an upper bulge.
row.turnaround: Not a big-mountain turnaround-time objective — the real time constraint is the 20-30 minute approach through Silver Basin and weather: the approach and buttress base are exposed, so turn back on the approach if lightning or fast-moving weather threatens before you're committed to the rock.
row.rappels: Single lower-off from chain anchors at the top.
row.comms: No documented cell coverage in this remote, forested Silver Basin approach off NF-9070; treat the area as a dead zone and carry a satellite messenger for emergencies.
row.descent: Lower off the chain anchor at the top of the route.

waypoints.name: FS Road 9070 Turnaround at Silver Basin

row.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 12 bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor. No trad gear needed.
what_to_bring: Helmet — rock at this new crag is still loose/sharp in places
Sturdy approach shoes for the talus/brush walk-in
Extra layer — Silver Basin can be cool and windy even in summer
pro_tips: Expect a full toolbox of technique in one pitch — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacks, jugs, crimps and underclings — so pace yourself for sustained variety rather than a single crux move.
Use the rest stance below the upper bulge (visible in the route's photos) to shake out before the final section.
watch_out: This is a newly-developed, "raw" crag — expect some loose or sharp holds and wear a helmet.
The NF-9070 access road is rough with sharp rocks and deep water bars; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended.
row.pro_needs: Sport rack only — 12 quickdraws (plus 1-2 extra for the anchor). No natural/trad protection required or possible.
row.best_season: June through October when FS Road 9070 is open and snow is minimal
row.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
row.descent_text: Single-pitch, fully bolted sport route with a chain lower-off anchor at the top; there is no walk-off. Clip/thread the chains and lower back to the base.
row.bail: Single-pitch and fully bolted — retreat simply means lowering off the last bolt clipped (leave a biner/draw behind if you can't otherwise clean while lowering).

pitch_detail.notes: Sustained, technically varied bolted pitch — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacks, jugs, crimps, underclings — 12 bolts to chain anchor; furthest-left line on the buttress.
